utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, there are two matters. One is that the -- we have been made aware through the Registrar of the Defence counsel's concern that LiveNote is not immediately available, and the -- we -- we -- because of the uncertainty of when it is likely to come up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Problem solved. It's on already. Which means that I can move to the second matter. The Chamber is in receipt of a motion yesterday to permit the testimony of a witness by videolink, and we inquire as to whether, A, the Defence intends to respond; and, if so, whether we would request an expedited response. Again, this is something that we -- we are not asking for an answer immediately but in the course of today Defence counsel could indicate where we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honours. If -- if you permit us, we will be able to give you an answer tomorrow? I mean, on the -- on the merit of the -- of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. Could you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, are we correctly advised that we should have anticipated an application from the Office of the Prosecutor in respect of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We just want to be safe. We only have an hour for this witness, who is a viva voce witness, and there may be some areas that we want to explore with this witness that will take us slightly over that. I don't anticipate much more time than the hour, but we do want to look at a couple of the log-books. And since this is our first judicial witness from the 1992 time-period as well as the first higher prosecutor from the time-period, we want to go over some organisational matters. And it might go a little bit beyond the hour, but we don't anticipate much beyond that. And I think with the cross-examination we still finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you begin by giving us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Staka Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, and what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19 October 1955. And I have a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you say you have a degree in law. Could you tell us in what capacity that you work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work as a judge of the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or at any trial in any of the countries of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The procedure before this Tribunal is one that you would not be unfamiliar with, in that it is -- it has features in common with any court anywhere in the world, with its own peculiarities, of course. You have been called by the Prosecution, and the -- as you would have heard in what has just passed between the Bench and counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Olmsted, they expect that their examination of you would take a little more than an hour. You would then be cross-examined by counsel for each of the two accused men, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin, and counsel for the first accused has requested two hours and counsel for the second accused an hour. And as Mr. Olmsted has said, we expect that your testimony would be completed within the compass of today. A sitting day for this Tribunal is ordinarily from 9.00 in the morning, which is the session we're beginning now, until 1.45 in the afternoon. The reason for that is that there are other trials going on, and the courtrooms have to be shared. That sitting day is divided into periods of not more than 90 minutes for technical reasons because tapes have to be changed and so on. So we would take two 20-minute breaks within the sitting day. Of course, if, for any reason, before the regular time of taking a break you need, for whatever reason, to indicate that -- that the Chamber needs to rise, you would let us know and we would accommodate you. And, unless there is any other area in which you have questions that I might answer, I would invite Mr. Olmsted to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first want to go rather quickly through your professional background. From 1980 until October 1983, you were a judge of the basic court in Sokolac; and then from 1985 until May 1992, you were a judge of the BiH Basic Court I in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after that, you were appointed judge of the basic court in Serb Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When were you appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The appointment happened on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long did you remain a basic court judge in Sarajevo, under that appointment?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Up to the 19th of December of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what position were you appointed to in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I was appointed as a senior prosecutor in Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I remained in that position up to December 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me clarify that. How long were you in the position of Sarajevo higher prosecutor? Was it -- the record says here until December 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: How many years -- for how many years were you a higher prosecutor for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: A little over two years. And I'm really confused now. I'm sorry. I believe that I remained in the position of senior prosecutor for a little over two years, or perhaps three. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I just wanted to clarify the years. Yes. Now, after you were a higher prosecutor, it's my understanding that you served as secretary of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska until approximately 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in 2001, you were appointed judge of the Serb Sarajevo district court; and in 2003, you were appointed to the RS Supreme Court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Correct. All of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2442.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 10 of the B/C/S, page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette of the Serbian People of BiH dated 30 June 1992. And if we can look at decision number 239, we see a 20 June 1992 decision by President Radovan Karadzic. Was this the decision appointing you to the basic court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you the only judge appointed to the Sarajevo basic court in June 1992, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I was not the only one. Some other judges were appointed on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall how many were appointed that day?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I believe that four were appointed for the basic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were judges for the higher court for Sarajevo also appointed at that time?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you recall how many higher court judges were appointed in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Six, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Also at this time, were the public prosecutor and deputy public prosecutors for Sarajevo basic prosecutor's office appointed?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, to the basic prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what were the ethnicities of these judges and prosecutors who were appointed in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: In June 1992, I believe that they were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where were the offices of the Sarajevo higher and basic court judges in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The main office was in Lukavica, on the premises of -- of the former administration building of Energoinvest; a company, Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were the offices of the Sarajevo basic prosecutor and his deputies located?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: At first, we shared the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were the offices of the centre for public security, the CSB for Romanija-Birac region, located.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, when we were given offices in Energoinvest, they were in a different building but within the same perimeter, the parameter of the Energoinvest building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When the basic court in Sarajevo was first established, over which municipalities did it have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Those were all the municipalities which had formally belonged to Sarajevo. And I'm referring to parts thereof. Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, Centar, and Vogosca, as well as Ilijas, Ilidza, Hadzici, and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at some point, were the Sarajevo basic court and basic prosecutor's offices divided into two?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When did this division occur; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I believe that that happened in Autumn 1992. But I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date. I don't know the date, although I believe that it was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after this division, which Sarajevo basic court and prosecutor's office had jurisdiction over crimes committed in Vogosca and Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The Basic Court II in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was that court located?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That court was located in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were additional judges and prosecutors appointed to the Basic Court and Prosecutor Office II in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Several persons were appointed at the time. Some prosecutors which were formerly appointed to work in the basic prosecutor's office were subsequently appointed as prosecutors in Ilidza. I'm referring to Milana Popadic, who was the deputy prosecutor in Sarajevo; and after the division, she was appointed the deputy prosecutor in the prosecutor -- Prosecutor's Office II in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to ask you some just very general procedural questions now. Looking back to 1992 and the procedures that existed then, when would have a judge such as yourself first become involved in a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: As soon as a public prosecutor issued an order for investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in order to conduct an investigation, what assistance did the judge need from the police?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: In the course of an investigation, if there was a need to locate certain individuals who were either suspects or potential witnesses or when information was needed, an investigating judge could request all those services from the police. For example, an investigative judge could order the police to check whether a person had a criminal record or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the judge wanted to have a search warrant or an arrest warrant executed, who would do that? Who would execute those warrants?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if the judge wanted some forensic analysis performed, either finger-print or ballistics or what have you, who would provide that forensic expertise?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: There were institutions that provided such expertise. And there were also forensic experts who provided different sorts of expertise. And a judge issued an order in which it was decided who would perform the expertise and what kind of expertise would be performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware, did the police perform any forensic analysis?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The police were able to perform some types of forensic analyses during the pre-criminal procedure, when data was collected, with a view to issuing a criminal report and preparations to launch a proper investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How many cases do you -- do you recall investigating as a basic court judge from June 1992 until you were appointed higher prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I was in charge of the investigation in one case; and in one case I was in charge of the first-instance procedure, the trial, once the indictment was issued. Maybe I can explain. An indictment could be issued for certain crimes without any prior investigation, which means that the prosecutor could issue an indictment immediately. And what followed was an immediate trial and conviction, or a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm really sorry, the -- I think this needs to be clarified because it will create a problem afterwards. I believe the witness was talking about the specific procedure which is called the "direct indictment," and it wasn't recorded. Therefore -- therefore, this has to be clarified because this is one of the options given by the law that you can directly indict somebody without the -- the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's talk about this first case. Council raised the issue. This was a case in which an indictment was issued directly without an investigation by an investigative judge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us just generally what kind of case this was?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The case was manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us the ethnicities of the perpetrator and the victim?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned the case went to trial. When did the trial occur?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. As far as I could remember, it was during the summer. The summer of 1992; I'm sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's talk about the second case that you worked on. Can you tell us what that case was about?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: In that case, the basic prosecutor issued a request to launch an investigation against Vladimir Srebrov for a crime pursuant to Article 118 of the then-Penal Code of the SFRY. He was taken into custody; he was remanded in custody. The prosecutor issued a request, and the case was handed over to me to carry out the investigation in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the ethnicity of Mr. Srebrov?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I believe that he was a Serb. Yes, I'm sure he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned Article 118 of the SFRY Criminal Code. Can you tell us what that provision is? What's the crime at stake?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact title of the crime, but it was to do with persuading people to join the enemy army; something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and where this crime took place?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, he was charged with acting in Sarajevo, with regard to his public appearances in Sarajevo, which was in the part under the Muslim control, and his arrival at Ilidza in order to discuss the cessation of hostilities. He arrived in Ilidza, and he had talks with some representatives of the Serbs there. Actually, he arrived at the police station in Ilidza, according to him. That's what he told us. And then he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He was arrested in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when did this occur; do you recall? When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I think it was in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you had an opportunity to review the case file. Do you recall who signed the police Official Note at the outset of the case?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I believe it was signed by Petko Budisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was Petko Budisa at the time?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, that document says that he was commander of that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall who from the RS MUP issued the initial remand order to detain this perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know why the minister of the interior himself issued the remand order in this case?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When did you receive the request from the prosecutor's office to initiate the investigation in this case? Approximately when?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: In September. I think it was the 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then, once you received that request, did you, in fact, conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I, of course, interviewed the accused, Vladimir Srebrov, and I issued a decision to launch an investigation, and I also signed an order for him to remain in custody for 30 days. The interview took two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall attending any meetings with police officers from the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I remember attending one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: At Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall roughly when did that meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you give us a season? Was it summer or fall?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: It was certainly summer, but I can't be more precise than that. It must have been at some time from June to September. It can't have been later. But I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who do you recall attended this meeting in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there were the representatives of the civilian police, the military police, and the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was --

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I interrupted the interpretation. Was there anything more to be interpreted? All right. I'll just move on then. Can you tell us, what was the purpose of this meeting in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to prevent - that's what I would call it - stealing vehicles from the perimeter of the factory at Vogosca. There was a large number of newly manufactured vehicles there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that the Tas car factory?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Tas factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the decision was taken for mixed patrols of the civilian police and the military police to guard the perimeter. This south-western part was completely cut off from the north-eastern part, and, therefore, the initiative was made to establish a separate court and public prosecutor's office for that area. It was then that people came up with this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why did you, as a judge, attend this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Ministry of Justice wanted somebody from the court to attend the meeting. And as far as I remember, they wanted somebody from the court because of the psychological effect, because it was all about preserving property and reducing the number of criminal offences. At least that's how it was explained to us. I don't remember why I was chosen to go; but, anyway, I went there as a representative of our court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than this one meeting in Vogosca, do you recall attending any other meetings with the police, either from the CSB Romanija-Birac or the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While you were a judge, between June and December 1992, do you recall any criminal cases initiated against Serb perpetrators for crimes committed against non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I never received such a file.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to turn to your position as a Sarajevo higher prosecutor. When you were a higher prosecutor, where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: My office was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where in Pale?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: At the Panorama Hotel, the administrative wing of that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which other government offices were located at that hotel?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The Supreme Court of the RS had its premises there at the time, as well as the public prosecutor's office of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was the republican prosecutor at that time?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Miroslav Godanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As higher prosecutor, which basic prosecutor's offices reported to you?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The Basic Prosecutor's Office I in Sarajevo, then number II in Sarajevo, then the basic prosecutor's office at Sokolac, Vlasenica, and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We already talked about how Vogosca and Ilijas were part of the Sarajevo Prosecutor Office II in Ilidza. Which prosecutor's office had jurisdiction over Pale?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The basic prosecutor's office from Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were a higher prosecutor, did the basic prosecutor's offices submit reports to you on their work?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. They submitted annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you also hold meetings in Pale with your basic prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember exactly whether we held meetings, and, if so, how many, because there were constant interruptions of communication lines with certain areas. But I went to the individual basic prosecutor's offices. And it would also happen that on the occasion of being sworn in, they would come to Pale. We didn't assemble all of us. But, on some occasions, I would meet with one prosecutor, or two, or three, but we didn't have plenary meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your two years as a Sarajevo higher prosecutor, do you recall receiving any reports about criminal charges brought against Serb perpetrators for committing crimes against non-Serb victims in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, if I may explain how the were reports made, the annual reports. An annual report contained information about the total number of criminal reports, what kind of decisions the prosecutor took pursuant to these reports, and the structure of crime -- criminal offences, which means that the names of the perpetrators were not mentioned. From those reports, one could see the results of the work of each prosecutor's office and the type of criminal offence committed in their area. Those reports did not contain any names. As for direct contact with those prosecutors, no prosecutor informed me specifically about what you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the level of the basic prosecutor's offices, what log-books were maintained of criminal reports received by those offices?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Log-books were maintained for some types of offences. They had their respective -- they were marked differently. KT included all criminal offences against known perpetrators. KTN stood for the log-book containing criminal reports against unknown perpetrators. KTM was how the log-book containing criminal reports against minor perpetrators was marked. And there was a fourth mark for the log-book containing information about the administrative duties of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the fourth log-book that you mentioned, that was the KTA?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As higher prosecutor, why was it important that the basic prosecutor's offices under your jurisdiction maintained these log-books?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: These log-books had always been maintained, before the war and after the war. Even now. They are an objective reflection of the activities of the prosecutor's office. It contains the basic information about all activities of a prosecutor's office as a governmental institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And would these log-books allow for the auditing of the work of the basic prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Of course. Because you can see everything there; what was done, how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to testifying here today, did you have the opportunity to review 1992 KT and KTN log-books, from Sarajevo, Sokolac, Vlasenica, and Visegrad Basic Prosecutor's Offices?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from each of those log-books, did you compile some statistics for us?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 10387 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, is this the statistical data that you collected from the KT and KTN log-books that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save time, I would propose to tender this document into evidence, and then I'll just ask a small handful of questions, general questions, regarding some of its data and some of the log-books that it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is opposed to this admission. This document is actually a reminder for the witness. This is not a document per se. The witness drafted this document, and, I suppose, following the instructions of my learned friend. If this document refers to the original documents in our possession and it is to be understood as a summary of those documents, then I see no reason why we shouldn't tender the original documents. Because, unless we do, there are -- there's no foundation for the allegations found in this document the Prosecutor wishes to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, to what end do you seek to -- to exhibit these summaries which the witness has made?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, the summaries are of log-books, prosecutor log-books, and I think you've had an opportunity to see a couple of them so far; they're rather large. To translate them all would be a tremendous effort for this Tribunal. And so it's much better to have a witness who has some familiarity with them and can testify about them as to what they contain. I certainly can go through all the information contained in this document that's in front of us right now; that's going to take a little bit of time. She's basically going to affirm the information into it -- in it because she created it and she signed it. And I think that doesn't really maximise the time of the this Trial Chamber for her to do so. I note that we've done the same practice with two other witnesses, Judge witnesses or prosecutor witnesses, and so I'm just following that precedent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we see the utility of the witness having compiled this synthesis of material herself. But the -- we -- in our view, Mr. Zecevic has correctly pointed out that that the limited utility of it is to assist the -- or to facilitate the examination and, I suppose, cross-examination of the witness in the box. The document by itself would have no use whatever as an exhibit, and I would even go so far as to say it, taken in isolation, would be misleading. So we understand the shortcut that you wish to take, but, unfortunately, this is one of those areas in which there is no getting around the fundamental material, bulky though it is, on which you would wish to rely. And the witness who is in the box could, I suppose, be asked questions about the summary that she would have presented and what specific items mean by way of example, but this cannot, in the Chamber's view, be admissible as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can take her through it, and I guess that's what I will have to do to come with the results of her analysis of these log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to the first log-book that you reviewed. You reviewed the Serb Sarajevo Prosecutor's Office 1992 KTA log-book. Can you tell us, what was date of the first entry you found in that log-book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have the indication of the document you are talking about, Mr. Olmsted? Does it have a name or tab number or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. This will be tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the date of the first entry in the KTA log-book?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Of the Sarajevo Prosecutor's Office? The 6th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but can we have the 65 ter number also so this can be shown to the -- to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It really --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll give the 65 ter numbers; but these are large log-books, and to load them all up in the system just so she can give her conclusions on that I think will take a lot of time. So let me just announce the 65 ter number, and they can take it from there. The 65 ter of this log-book was 2956.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you also reviewed the Ilidza Prosecutor's Office 1992 KT log-book. What was the date of the first entry you found in that log-book?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is -- this is 65 ter 2955.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The 1st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the total number of criminal reports received by that office between 1 April and 31 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The total number of criminal reports is 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we talked about how the Prosecutor's Office II in Sarajevo was created sometime in November of 1992. So does this entry, this first entry, conform with, basically, your understanding of when that prosecutor's office was created?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. You also reviewed the Sokolac Prosecutor's Office 1992 KT log-book. What was the date of the first entry found after 1 April 1992 in that log-book?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 1544.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many entries -- how many criminal reports were received by this office between 1 April and 31 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, I'm really sorry. The accused are protesting because they cannot follow any -- any -- anything. They don't get any kind of information, what Mr. Olmsted is directing the witness about. Because what we have on the -- on the screen is, I believe, the first document. We are now on the third log-book. And we still have the first log-book on the -- on the ELMO. I'm just saying this for the purposes of the accused. The accused should be able to follow, at the very least, what is going on -- and what documents is -- are the parties referring to. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure I understand the utility in bringing up the log-books. We certainly can. But this witness is saying when the first entry was and how many entries are in the log-book. I think that that is something that would require -- you know, I'm not sure what the Defence wants us to do; flip through each page and count them for ourselves? Or can this witness simply divulge what she found when she reviewed these log-books?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I suppose the alarm of the accused is understandable. But isn't the -- don't we come back to what the Chamber would have indicated to Mr. Olmsted when we started down this path? That what we are really concerned about is the oral testimony of the witness on the basis of what she would have examined; and the back documents, as it were, are -- have -- obviously form the basis of the line of questions. But what we should all, including the accused, concentrate on, are the specific questions that counsel is now putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all -- with all due respect, I -- I fully understand and appreciate the position of the Trial Chamber, and I understand the position of my learned friend. However, if, for example, Mr. Olmsted is asking the witness to confirm which is the first date in the log-book and she confirms a certain date, it is -- it is a couple of seconds that, before that, Mr. Olmsted says 65 ter 1554, page 1. So the accused can see actually that the witness is reading the actual date where -- where it's -- what is written in the log-book. That is my opinion that it would be only fair to the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it seems to -- to us that it only adds a layer of confusion to be showing these documents, which we don't see, at the end of this present exercise, being exhibited in any event. To repeat what I said earlier, what we are concentrating on is the witness's oral evidence. Admittedly, that her -- what she would say is based on the documents that she would have examined. She has already said that; that's a part of the record. But it only, as I said, adds confusion to -- to be running these documents on the screen, which we don't see, at the end -- we have already said that the summary would not be admissible, and we don't see the log-books being admitted either. As you have said, they are, A, voluminous, and, B, haven't all been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But it is important to our case to get this information in, and I think this is by far the most expedient way of doing it. The Defence will have the opportunity to question any information she derived from these log-books, and they can do it through this witness or they can do it through any future witness. Or they can file something otherwise to -- to question the -- the veracity of her calculations. But these are, you know, such basic information, based upon a review, that to bring up the log-book and to confirm everything she's determined from them will -- it would just, I think, needlessly take the time of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know if we're at cross purposes, Mr. Olmsted. We're inviting you to continue asking her questions. And it is the duty of counsel on both sides to, at some point, seek to match those questions to the basic documents, which are the log-books. But what we are saying is that while you're asking her questions we don't need to have the log -- these documents put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I understand you, Your Honour. I apologise for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also -- Judge Gojkovic, you also had the opportunity to review the Vlasenica Prosecutor's Office 1992 KT log-book. Can you tell us, what was the date of the first entry in that log-book on or after 1 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The date is 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the total number of criminal reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Again, we don't have a 65 ter number. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if I may be of assistance, it seems to me that the summary which this witness has put together and which is now -- which was offered by the Prosecution contains nothing more than figures relating to the date of the beginning of the log-book and the number of crimes that were registered. The Defence, of course, is free challenge the correctness of what the witness has put together. If there is a challenge, say, against the number of crimes that were registered in Ilidza and you're able to prove that it wasn't 46 crimes, it was only 44 crimes, then, of course, you should do so. But at this point in time in the Prosecution's chief examination, I guess the interest is not so much about ascertaining the number of crimes or the correctness of the information which the witness has offered in this summary, but, rather, the breakdown of the numbers. Because, as Judge Hall, the Presiding Judge, has already said, in isolation this information is useless, unless we get a breakdown of numbers: Out of the 46 crimes registered in Ilidza, how many crimes were -- were concerning Muslim perpetrators, how many were concerning Serb perpetrators, who were the victims, what was the charge, and so on. So that is, I think, in the end, the information that the Chamber is looking for. So as much as I understand your -- your unhappiness with the fact that we don't see the underlying material, I think at this point in time we can proceed without having to use time to go into each and every one of these log-books and confirm and ascertain that the number of crimes that the witness has offered in her summary is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours' position, and I appreciate it very much. I'm just trying to explain the two things. Number one, for the record, we need the 65 ter number of the document that the witness is referring to. I think that's only logical. We can't -- we can't play with the tab numbers, because the tab numbers do not appear anywhere else. They are just for the purposes of our facilitating work in the courtroom. That is why I insisted that the 65 ter number is always used; so I know what is the document and we know in the record afterward. The -- the problem I see, Your Honours, is that this doesn't help saving the time. It -- it only - it only - increases the time. Because Mr. Olmsted prepared this summary document last night. He sends it to us with the data which is -- which Your Honours correctly suggested are the numbers and the -- the qualification of some of the criminal -- criminal filings. Now, we are going to challenge that. Of course we are going to challenge that. Because there is no basis for these conclusions from the documents which -- which are -- which are before us. And now we will have to go through each and every entry in these log-books to show the Trial Chamber that the witness did not have the basis to confirm this. Now it will take maybe two days. Instead that the Prosecution, who has the burden of proof, shows the document, shows the -- shows the example on which they base their -- their -- their assertion that the witness is -- has -- on the basis of which the witness has created this document. That is all I'm saying. Nothing else. And I think, with all due respect, I think the Defence position is very justified in this respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I wasn't in any way trying to say that you were not justified in -- in bringing up ... it's just that I'm surprised that the very limited information which is contained in the witness's summary can actually be challenged. I mean, is that -- was the witness wrong in providing the information that in Ilidza from 1st of April to 31st December there were 46 crimes registered? I mean, is that the challenge? Or where does the challenge come in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness should be excused before I answer that question, or maybe the witness can be withdrawn before the time. Or we are about the time to break, so maybe the witness can be excused and can I answer that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Gojkovic, we are near the time that we would ordinarily take a break. The usher will escort you from the courtroom at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- rather than -- Mr. Zecevic, rather than your continuing your representation to the Chamber at this point, it seems that the more efficient thing - it mightn't work out - may be if counsel, during the break, could see if a practical solution to this very real problem can be worked out. Because we appreciate what you -- what -- what both counsel have said, and it may very well -- it -- it appears that the Prosecution may not have anticipated the problems that would have been created by the shortcut, what they thought would have been a shortcut. So if counsel can get together during the break and report back when we resume as to whether there is anything that they have to offer as -- as to how we go forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the witness is escorted back to the stand, the Chamber would wish to -- unless, of course, counsel have something to report about progress they would have made. So let's hear from counsel first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we spoke with Defence counsel, and I think it was primarily a misunderstanding. We're not going seek to tender this document into evidence; we're simply having her use it to refresh her recollection based upon a review of the log-books. I certainly will note the 65 ter number of the log-book. We won't put it on the screen, though. And I think that that was acceptable to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- basically we -- I understood that the -- the Prosecution offered this document, and -- and that was -- that was the basis of my objection. The other objections were concerning the 65 ter. Now, the Prosecution assures me that they're interested in this document in number one and two, which is the first date of entry and the number of entries for 1992, which I don't have a problem with. The problem I have is under number three and four, but my friend from the Prosecution explained me that he is going to ask the witness directly for her opinion on that. And that is basically okay with us. Thank you, Your Honours. I hope this satisfies the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is -- Mr. Zecevic, what is on the three and four? Or, Mr. Olmsted, what is on the three and four? We don't have the document anymore on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The number three is the total number of the criminal complaints concerning non-Serbs by -- committed by Serbian perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the number four is also related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Olmsted explained to me that he is going ask the witness a question, therefore, and is he not going to rely on this document. So we'll see what this witness will answer, and then we will cross-examine on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, could you give us an indication as to the -- the purpose of these questions, these precise questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's two-fold. The ones I'm asking her, with regard to the statistical sheet, is establishing that the prosecutor's offices were open for business in 1992, they were accepting criminal reports, and several of them processed quite a few of them. That's what I'm going to use the statistical sheet for. I will ask her, generally, what her -- what she found. With regard to number three, I'm not going refer her to the sheet, I going to ask her, just outright, based upon a review of these log-books, was she able to identify any cases in which the Serb was a perpetrator and a non-Serb was a victim. And we'll hear her answer at that stage on that. Based upon her looking at these seven or eight log-books. And I note that's exactly what we did with two witnesses who have testified here already. So it's simply -- there -- she's the higher prosecutor; these log-books fell within her purview because they were her basic prosecutors who were collecting this information and maintaining these log-books which were used for auditing purposes and which were the basis of reports going up the chain of command, and she, simply, has reviewed them and told us what she's been able to find in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would have the witness back. If the usher would please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Judge Gojkovic, we apologise for the delay. We just had to deal with a couple of procedural matters. I want to return to the results of your review of the log-books. We were talking about the Vlasenica Prosecutor's Office 1992 KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Which I just note for the record is 65 ter 1552.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based upon your review, the total number of criminal reports received by that prosecutor's office between 1 April and 31 December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: 191 criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the Visegrad Prosecutor's Office 1992 KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I note for the record this is 65 ter 1550.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based upon your review, what was the date of the first entry in that log-book on or after 1 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: 9 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the total number of criminal reports received by that office between 1 April and 31 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you also looked at the Ilidza Prosecutor's Office 1992 KTN log-book. Can you tell us, what was the total number of unknown perpetrator criminal reports received between 1 April and 31 December 1992 by that office?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, for the record, that's 65 ter 2969.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also reviewed the Vlasenica Prosecutor's Office 1992 KTN log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 2968.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us the total number of unknown perpetrator criminal reports received by that office between 1 April and 31 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, the Visegrad Prosecutor's Office 1992 KTN log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 2971.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the total number of unknown perpetrator criminal reports received between 1 April and 31 December 1992 by that office?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: From your review of the 1992 KTN -- or strike that. From your review of the 1992 KT log-books, were you able to identify any criminal reports filed by the police for crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from your review of the three 1992 KTN log-books, were you able to identify any criminal reports for crimes against non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When the Serb Sarajevo Prosecutor's Office was located solely in Lukavica, so before the split in November of 1992, did the prosecutor's office maintain a KT log-book?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Our investigators were unable to locate this log-book. Can you tell us what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what happened to it. But I do know that this prosecutor's office had transferred its offices to Grbavica and that the premises where they were originally located were shelled. I don't know whether they were destroyed, whether it was destroyed, their log-book. I don't know what may have happened to it. I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at 65 ter 10385. This is a request to initiate an investigation dated 7 September 1992. And we've already talked about this Srebrov case in which you were investigative judge. I just want you to take a look at the upper left of the first page. We see written "KT 24/92." Could you tell us, what is the purpose of that number?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: This number shows the sequence of these criminal reports that were entered into the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So as of the beginning of September 1992, how many criminal reports were received by the Serb Sarajevo Basic Prosecutor's Office, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: According to this number here, this is the 24th criminal report. For this log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2955. This will be the 1992 through 1993 Sarajevo Basic Prosecutor's Office II KT log-book. And while we're pulling that up, did you also review, during proofing, the 1993 entries in the KT log-book from the Sarajevo Basic Prosecutor's Office II?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Only for the Sarajevo Basic Prosecutor's Office II.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's right. And were you able to identify any cases in the 1993 KT log-book against a Serb perpetrator for a crime committed against a non-Serb victim, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: There was one case that was entered in 1993, and the criminal report bore the date of, I think, December 1992. The perpetrator was a Serb, and the damaged parties were described as members of "other nationalities."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at page 23 of the B/C/S and page 6 of the English. And if we can zoom in to the last entry on the page; I believe it's entry 30. And zoom in a little bit more on the B/C/S so she can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Judge Gojkovic, is this the case that you identified, this entry number 30?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the name of the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Stanko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when was the criminal report received by the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The 9th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's scroll over to column 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, move -- move -- scroll over in the B/C/S. No, not up; over. Yeah. Now keep on going. Keep on going. Okay. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to this log-book, what happened to this case in 1995?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: It says here that the investigation was interrupted. It was dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge why the investigation was interrupted or dropped?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: It was just interrupted. It was not ended. And I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than this one case that you identified, were you able to identify any other criminal reports of crimes committed in 1992 by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims in this 1993 KT log-book?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there were examples where victims are not even identified. There are no names of the victims in any of the log-books that I reviewed. The one in 2003 [as interpreted] shows another example where the victim was a woman who bore a Serbian family name and her first name was not Serbian, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, was that crime committed in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this log-book be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to show you one more document and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. As Exhibit P1445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have on the screen P275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, could you repeat the 65 ter number of this log-book we just admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. It's 2955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Judge Gojkovic, what we're looking at now is the minutes from the 8th Session of the RS Presidency, dated 17 June 1992. If we look at number 3, it states: "The following conclusion was adopted: That the government draft a decision on the establishment of a state documentation centre which will gather all genuine documents on crimes committed against the Serbian People during this war." Do you recall whether this documentation centre was, in fact, established?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was responsible for collecting this documentation?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, Miroslav Toholj was -- I don't know whether he was appointed its director or whether he bore a different title. The documentation centre organised a collection of all the documents, and I believe that he was in charge of the overall organisation of setting up a team that would be working on collecting all those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether the police played any role in collecting documents --or documenting the crimes committed against the Serb population, for the centre?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I'm wondering whether it would be beneficial to mark the log-books that this witness summarised as exhibits at this stage, until we can figure out the best means of -- of whether we need to tender themselves into evidence or whether it's going to be acceptable to have them summarised. But at least to have them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, you do mean marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's right; marked for identification. I could provide a list to the Registrar, and they could just assign P numbers for them. And then at least we know they're on the -- they're in the record, and we can figure out what's the best way to get this evidence in, if it's necessary at all to get it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't this premature, Mr. Olmsted? We see the practical aspect of your application. But isn't this premature? Because the -- inasmuch as the log-books have not yet all been translated, the -- I think that's as far as we can go for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, a few of them have, that she reviewed -- well, partially translated, let's say. We'll never get them fully translated just because some of them are quite large. But she did review them, and she did testify about them, and we did announce their 65 ter numbers on the record. So I was thinking maybe this would be a good time to do that. But if the Trial Chamber is of the opinion to wait, we'll address the matter later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But although she reviewed them, they're still merely foundation documents for her viva voce testimony. And I -- I think that's where they should be left for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, first of all, about our Criminal Code and criminal procedure. I would like to clarify a few things with this regard. According to our criminal procedure - and when I say "our," I mean the procedure that was in place in 1992, which is relevant for this indictment - the police filed criminal reports whenever there was reasonable grounds to suspect that a person committed a crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the police, of course, such a criminal report is filed with the competent prosecutor's office; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the police, citizens also had the right, and even an obligation, and I believe that was stipulated by the law, to file criminal reports; am I right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the police or citizens filed a criminal report or when they reported a crime and when they specified the type of the crime that was committed, such a specification in no way limited the prosecutor to file a request to investigate the crime, such as committed in the eyes of the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify. If, for example, somebody filed a criminal report -- for example, the police did that for an aggravated theft, whereas, the facts established, during the so-called pre-trial procedure conducted by the police, indicate that the crime is -- can be characterised as a robbery, then the prosecutor will follow the logic and will charge the perpetrator with the more serious crime - robbery in this case - irrespective of the fact that the initial criminal report was filed for an aggravated robbery -- aggravated theft; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the interpretation, we have to make pauses between my questions and your answers. I thank you kindly for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, after the prosecutor reviewed the documents provided to him by the police, together with the criminal report, or a citizen, a victim, who could also file a criminal report, and then the prosecutor filed a request for investigation and based it on his view that there were reasonable grounds to believe that a certain individual had committed a crime, which the prosecutor specified in their written request submitted to the investigative judge. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once a request for investigation is filed, the investigating judge will decide whether there are grounds for the investigation to be launched; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when the request for investigation is handed over to the investigating judge the investigating judge agrees that there should be an investigation of a case or of an individual, from that moment on, the dominus, to put it that way, the main person, the person in charge in the proceedings, is undoubtedly the investigating judge; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge has a certain body of rights which include and which he is duty-bound to issue for the enforcement agencies to carry out concern actions every time upon his specific order; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Within the scope of the investigation, the police -- or, rather, the bodies of the -- of interior affairs, do not act on their own will; they act either on the order of the investigating judge or the prosecutor. In other words, at the request of the prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. After the criminal report was filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is also, is it not, madam, that if a serious crime was committed and the duty investigating judge and the duty prosecutor go to the site immediately after that crime had taken place to carry out an on-site investigation, from that moment on, effectively, both the investigating judge and the prosecutor provide instructions to the police as to what to do; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's because, effectively, the presence of an investigating judge and the prosecutor on the crime scene is the beginning of an investigation. An order is issued. But the fact that they came to the site, in case of a serious crime, violent death, or any such situations, such a development, constitutes the launching of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: These are investigative actions that precede, following procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really glad that you mentioned "investigative actions." The fact is that some crimes which one might call the less serious crimes - and I'm again talking about the year 1992 and the regulations that were in effect at the time - for all those less serious crimes, and I believe that they were qualified by a prison sentence of up to three years, there was no investigation as such. Actually, what happened was investigative actions were carried out in order to establish whether there were elements and reasons for proceedings to be initiated against a certain person; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. Only certain actions were undertaken that were absolutely indispensable to proceed, an indictment with a lesser or milder effect. That was just an indictment proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- although the interpreters haven't so indicated, I get the impression that the gap between the question and the answer isn't sufficiently long. So if both the witness and counsel would bear that in mind, the need for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two of us speak the same language, and we are rightfully inclined to follow each other immediately; but both my question and your answer have to be recorded, hence the need for a short break. At the beginning of your testimony earlier today, you referred to a case where a direct indictment was issued. And you were the presiding judge in that case, in 1992. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in the proceeding that preceded that indictment, although this crime was a serious crime, the facts were very clear. And I assume that only some investigative actions were undertaken, and the prosecutor, after that, directly charged the person, without launching a proper investigation; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one specific matter. Since you worked both -- also as a prosecutor for a while, a prosecutor who was not happy or satisfied with the contents of the criminal report he is seized with, he could propose that certain investigative actions be taken so as to establish whether there was, indeed, reasonable grounds to suspect that a certain perpetrator committed a certain crime; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A prosecutor also had a possibility to do the following: When he received a criminal report, he could turn to the police -- or, rather, before he even received a criminal report, when he received information that a certain crime had been committed, the prosecutor's office could request from the police to collect the -- the so-called preliminary information; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, there was a special log-book, the so-called P.O. log-book for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you will agree with me that in any case every such prosecutor's request for an action by the police had to be recorded somewhere; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I'm sure you're right. It must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in such a case, when the prosecutor's office requested preliminary information to be gathered, they also provided the enforcement bodies with a set of instructions as to who they were interested in, which additional information about certain persons had to be gathered, about what facts, the time-frame, the place, and so on and so forth; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we saw that the prosecutor's office is not bound in any way by the legal qualification used by the body of the Ministry of the Interior or the person filing the criminal report, except with respect to the facts; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is, the public prosecutor can freely decide which criminal offence he will state in the request to conduct an investigation and, after that, in the indictment. And that is at the discretion of the prosecutor, which is based on the facts that have been established in the procedure until that time, which make the prosecutor think that there are reasonable grounds to suspect that such a crime has been committed and that it can be proved before a court of law; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the file makes it to court - that is, when the indictment enters into legal force and a court hearing starts - after the hearing, the court is supposed to decide. It is a fact, isn't it, that the trial chamber that makes the decision is not bound by the prosecutor's qualification in the indictment, but, rather is only bound by the facts stated in that indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In essence, that means that the trial chamber can convict a person of a crime if the trial chamber thinks that it has been proved during the hearing that this crime was committed. That crime, however, must not be the same as the one that the prosecutor states in the indictment -- need not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Need not," rather than -- "must not."

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I apologise, I'm trying to control the transcript. So, if an indictment is issued for the crime of qualified murder, aggravated murder, and during the hearing before court it is established that there are elements of another offence, such as a war crime, then the court can pronounce that person guilty of committing a war crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, if the facts of the criminal offence are all the relevant facts that prove that the person has, indeed, committed what he or she is charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I believe we have clarified as much. The court is bound by the facts from the indictment rather than by the legal qualification. That's the essence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I won't show it to you because I believe it isn't necessary; but for the sake of reference, it is P119. That's the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of BiH. Madam, in 1992, there was, still, the death penalty in the legislation of that republic; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. And even later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was certainly the most severe sentence; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out to you to remind you. In the second part of chapter 6 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was applied in the territory of the Republika Srpska in 1992 also, Article 36 describes the offence of murder. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And murder, in paragraph 2, is -- or, rather, paragraph 2 describes aggravated murder, and the sentence -- punishment for that is ten years at least, and the severest sentence is the death penalty; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then the types and descriptions of various types of aggravated murders is listed: Item 1 is in a cruel or insidious way; then item 2, whoever deprives somebody else of his or her life, and, with premeditation, jeopardizes the life of another person; and then recklessness; then authorised officials; then several persons. And so on. Do you remember, so I needn't read it out?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of another criminal offence from Article 151. I'm again referring to the Law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which in 1992 was also applied in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I said, the Article in question is 151, that deal with severe cases of robbery or -- robbery and theft combined with robbery. And Article 2 describes a qualified type of that offence; namely, a situation when, during the performance of a robbery, a person is deprived of his or her life with premeditation. And, in that case, that offence is punishable by at least ten years, up to the death sentence?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that is an aggravated form of that criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is the following -- or, rather, what I would like to you confirm, and I hope you will: It's a fact, isn't it, that under the rules and regulations in force at the time, the most severe sentence is the death penalty, and it could be imposed, as we have just seen, in these two cases; and the same sentence, the most severe one, could be imposed also for war crime, crimes against humanity -- or, rather, it was a sentence stipulated by the law for these offences. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So from the aspect of penalties, the law does not distinguish between persons indicted of some type of qualified murders or a type of aggravated robbery or crimes against humanity; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Not with regard to the sanctions envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You may remember that at the very outset of your evidence today you were asked by my learned friend about an investigation that you conducted as investigating judge in 1992 against Vladimir Srebrov. Do you remember?
