utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then the Prosecutor suggested to you, and you accepted, as you have already stated in your answer, that the decision to place that person in remand was signed by the minister of the interior, Mr. Mico Stanisic. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 65 ter document 10383 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something, Ms. Gojkovic: Did you ever receive any document from Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: No. At least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please enlarge the section of the document that contains the signature. This is the document shown to you by the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, here we see the title typed out: "Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic." But take a look at the stamp. We can see that inside the stamp there is the letter Z. I believe that it stands for "za," 4, and it's followed by a signature. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Inside the stamp, there is a character. And the signature itself is difficult to read. I saw what was typed on -- on the typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, madam, that this is not Mico Stanisic's signature but, rather, that of Mr. Tomislav Kovac, who had met this gentleman, Mr. Srebrov, to talk with him about some things.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That's not for me to know. I'm not saying that he signed it in person. I only said that I cannot read the signature. However, I could read, or I was able to read, what was typewritten, and I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10384.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's an Official Note concerning the same case, the case against Vladimir Srebrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please enlarge the signatures in the lower right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm objecting to what I anticipate will be the line of questioning here. I think that my learned friend is going to ask this witness to compare signatures on two different documents to determine whether that is, in fact, the signature of Mr. Stanisic. I think the most appropriate way to do this would to be tender the two documents into evidence and let the Trial Chamber compare the signatures. I don't see why this witness is an expert in handwriting or anything else. She's said that she's not familiar with Mr. Stanisic's signature; she's saying that she's not seen that he, in fact, signed it. I so I think that's really the end of the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the question hasn't been asked yet. Perhaps we should allow Mr. Zecevic to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, madam, that this document is signed by - at least that's what it says, and I'm not sure you can see it - it is signed by two persons, and the typewritten names are Tomislav Kovac and Petko Budisa. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender both these documents into evidence: 65 ter 10383 and 65 ter 10384.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To establish what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To establish that the allegation that Mico Stanisic signed these -- this -- the document on remand -- the decision on remand, as suggested by the Prosecutor, as -- and as confirmed by the witness, which is 65 ter 10383, is basically not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm certain it isn't peculiar to the system -- to the Rules of Evidence and the system of law with which -- from which I come, the rule of presumption of regularity. There is a document, which is -- will not be disputed as an official document, and it's issued in the name of the minister. It is a matter for the internal administration of the department at the time as to whether he manually signed it or somebody signed it for him, which I understand to be the purpose for which the Prosecution was tendering the document. I didn't understand - and perhaps Mr. Olmsted will tell me if I misunderstood the purpose of his line of questioning - that he -- it is was being tendered for the witness to establish that the minister personally signed the document because I don't understand anything to turn on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honours. That is precisely why I am challenging this. Because he said, Mr. Olmsted said, to the witness, he proposed to the witness that Mr. Stanisic has signed this document and even asked the witness, Why do you think Mr. Stanisic signed the decision on remand? So he is suggesting and the -- and the -- very strongly suggesting that it was actually signed by Mr. Stanisic. And that is what I say is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm just going back to record, page 12 of the transcript today, and I'm actually quite pleased the Trial Chamber was listening closely to my questions. I did say: "Do you recall who from the RS MUP issued the initial remand ... to detain this perpetrator? "A. Mico Stanisic did. "Do you know why the minister of interior himself issued the remand order?" I didn't say anything about his signing it. It's in his name, as Your Honour has just pointed out. It's -- it can be presumed that it came from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure that I remember where we are now, in terms of the issue before the -- the Chamber. It's 12.08. We would return to this when -- when we come back. Because it seems to me, from what has passed between the Bench and counsel, that there is not an issue. But I suppose your application -- there is no real issue, let me put it that way, and I don't mean to be disrespectful to counsel in respective cases when I say that. But your application was to tender these two documents as exhibits, as I recall, Mr. Zecevic? And I come back --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and I come back to the question as, To what end? Because, at bottom, what we are left with are documents which would have been issued on the authority of the -- of the minister who would have been responsible; unless, of course, it is a part of your case that these are wholly fictitious documents, which takes us down another path altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we and the Prosecutor are in agreement about that. Because it is not the responsibility of the minister to issue decisions on remand. Not at all. Therefore -- therefore, the -- the -- therefore, that is why Mr. Olmsted was suggesting -- was asking the witness, Why do you think minister himself ordered the -- the remand of this -- of this person? And I say, It wasn't minister at all, and it wasn't done on his authority at all. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll take the break and come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I have several corrections to the transcript from last Friday. On page 11647, the exhibit number should read 1D324. On page 11650, the exhibit number should be 1D325. And on page 11674, the exhibits admitted are P1430 through P1445. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 44, I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In order -- sorry, Mr. Olmsted, you had something to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to clarify, when Mr. Zecevic left off at the end of last session, he said that the Prosecutor and the Defence were in agreement that the minister didn't have any authority to issue remand decisions, and I just want to clarify that there is no agreement on that. That is not the position of the Prosecutor. Nor is it the reason why I asked the follow-up question as to why the minister had issued that remand decision. I just want to clarify that there is no agreement on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what we understood the question to be at the time, was the -- even if Mr. Olmsted over-spoke, as it were, in terms of, say, emphasizing the -- the -- the minister having signed the order in question, the ordinary rule of the presumption of regularity of official acts, which goes by the Latin idiom omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta, means that if Mr. Zecevic is challenging that presumption, it means that there would be cast a persuasive burden on him evidentially, and in order to -- it would seem to us that that is the only basis under which he could be seeking to ask to tender these documents, because he is intending to prove that the documents are fictitious. Otherwise we don't see how the question of admitting them arises. There is the ancillary consideration that it is somewhat curious, in terms of the first document, which -- which was signed on behalf of the minister, that the Prosecution couldn't have tendered it -- well, I shouldn't say couldn't - didn't seek to tender, it not being on their 65 exhibit list, that -- that counsel for the Defence would seek to do so now. So in order to consider the application of the Defence to tender these two documents, we want be to be clear that Mr. Zecevic is -- his application is based on the recognition that if his challenge is to the -- that these documents are wholly irregular, as being wholly fictitious, it would be necessary for him to state that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Your Honours -- Your Honours, I don't know if I can be of -- of assistance to the point which I feel the Trial Chamber expects me to. Your Honours, we say, first of all, that this order is not the order on remand. This is a completely different situation. It says, on the face of it, it says the order of remand, but it's not. And I'm going to explore that with the -- with the witness. I say -- we say that the minister does not have the authority for that and that -- that the signature is not the minister's and that in no way was minister -- has minister authorised this person to sign this document, the person who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- Mr. -- Mr. Olmsted had anticipated something that you were about to -- to -- which he thought you were about to do. In terms of the second document, would you be going so far as to invite the witness to compare the signatures on the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I agree with the -- I agree with -- with Mr. Olmsted and the witness because the witness said herself, I cannot recognise the signatures, because she never saw the signature of Mico Stanisic. She confirmed that in my cross-examination. And, of course, she's not an expert. I just wanted to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber because it's clearly that these two -- these two signatures are -- are pretty much similar, and it refers to Mr. Tomislav Kovac. And, if need be, we will lead evidence in our Defence case to that respect. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the first document is admitted as an exhibit, and you would ask the witness such questions that you consider useful to your case on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very, very much, Your Honours. So just for the clearness of the record, it's 65 ter 10383.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This will become Exhibit 1D326.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Gojkovic, just one more question about this document, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D326, 65 ter 10383; that's the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In a minute you are going to see it on the screen, and I would invite your comments upon it. Madam, this decision to remand somebody in custody is actually a decision on remand, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to the prevalent regulations, the police could remand a suspect in custody, a potential perpetrator, up to three days, up to 72 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, that person had to be brought before the competent investigative judge who, upon the proposal of the public prosecutor, could extend the custody for a period of up to a month; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The one -- the period of one-month custody ordered by the investigative judge can be extended up to a maximum of six months, upon the proposal of both the investigating judge and the public prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. That can be done by the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation we heard is "trial chamber;" however, we're talking about a special chamber which existed in all the courts pursuant to the then-organisation of work. However, the gist of the matter is that the chamber that decided on keeping somebody in custody for an extended period of time also acted upon the proposal of an investigating judge; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Upon the proposal of an investigating judge and the public prosecutor. And that was done during the stage of the investigation. It could be done up to the moment when the investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same chamber that decided on remanding somebody in custody also decided on the objections and proposals to abolish somebody's custodial sentence upon the proposal of a defence team?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, the gist of the matter was this: Once a person was remanded in custody for up to 72 hours, the police could not keep that person for any longer. During that period of time, such a person had to be brought before the investigating judge who, in turn, instituted different measures upon the proposal of a -- the competent public prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That was the law in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a brief question. On page 35, lines 18 and 19, I believe, the Prosecutor showed you P275, which is a -- actually a record or the minutes of a Presidency session. We are going to have it on the screen in a minute to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I remember the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor invited your comment on bullet point 3 in this document, whereby the Presidency ordered the government to prepare a decision on the establishment of the State Documentation Centre which would be in charge of collecting authentic documents about crimes committed against the Serbian People in the course of the war. You said that you're familiar with this decision and that, as far as you know, Mr. Toholj was in charge of that documentation centre; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it true that this State Documentation Centre, which gathered documents on crimes committed against the Serbian People, focussed primarily on crimes committed in the territory under the control of the Muslim and Croatian forces and not on the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I never paid a visit to that documentation centre, so I don't have any direct knowledge about its functioning. However, what I heard and read in the media and what I'm reading here under bullet point 3, that documentation centre would be operational in the areas where crimes were committed against the Serbs, whether those areas were constantly under the control of the enemy side or temporarily taken over by the Serb side. One would say that you're right. I only know about Presenica [phoen] village near Trnovo. I know that at one point in time, when the enemy side entered that village, crimes were committed, and I saw a photo documentation. But not in my formal capacity, but, rather, in my private capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam -- I apologise. Do you know that the Nationality Security Service particularly dealt with crimes committed against Serbs -- or, rather, they collected information about crimes committed against Serbs in the territory that was not under the control of the military or the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. The Nationality Security Service was engaged in those activities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This certainly doesn't mean that crimes committed against other ethnic groups in the territory of Republika Srpska would not be documented or processed, prosecuted; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I think that they should all be documented and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to show you 1D84. This letter was written by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to all public security centres in the territory of Republika Srpska. It is dated 5 June 1992. The signatory is the assistant minister for prevention and detection of crime, Mr. Dobro Planojevic. Did you have an occasion to possibly see this document before I showed it to you? Are you familiar with Mr. Dobro Planojevic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I knew Dobro Planojevic even before the war, and I know that he was assistant minister in 1992. I don't believe I have seen this particular document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, Mr. Dobro Planojevic, about halfway through the text, appeals to the best possible cooperation with the judicial bodies and the police in the efforts to combat crime. Do you think that there were attempts to bring about such cooperation?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Could you please explain your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else so as not to waste time. You will see from the text that Mr. Planojevic insists that things must be documented. He literally says: "Special attention it to be paid to uncovering perpetrators of war crimes ... Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in the last-but-one sentence, he says -- and I would like to hear your comment on that. He says: "In war time, you will encounter numerous obstacles in combatting crime and will, on occasion, be unable to take adequate measures. In such cases, you are to record all information in Official Notes for subsequent measures, that is, criminal prosecution." Madam, this means, doesn't it, that in cases when, due to war-time activities, it's impossible to conduct an on-site investigation and other activities that, under the law and regulations of the MUP, must be carried out, at least an Official Note must be drafted to make it possible for a subsequent investigation to be carried out, once the conditions allow that, in accordance with the regulations in force for and applying to the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior. Is that the way you understood it?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The -- my learned friend is asking the witness to interpret a document she never saw from the police which she was not a part of. It doesn't seem like there is a sufficient foundation. She's obviously answered the question, but I just raise my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, the witness is -- was a prosecutor at the time, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move -- let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, it's a fact, isn't it, that under the regulations in force at the time, war crimes and crimes against humanity, that, for them, there was no statute of limitations?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice of the RS was being established in April 1992. That's when it began; right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I don't know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I followed your testimony attentively and remember all the relevant facts, then you were appointed judge in June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you P1318.23. That's a -- an activity report for -- of the Ministry of Justice and Administration, dated May 10 1992, for -- for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: For May through October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had the opportunity to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Do you mean in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at any time before this testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. Before this testimony I did, but not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show page 2 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that at the very beginning it says that the Ministry of Justice and Administration began functioning in extremely complex conditions due to the well-known war-related events. And then it goes on to speak on the establishment of the rule of law and legal security of the citizens. And apart from the Supreme Court and the public prosecutor's office, a total of -- a number of courts and other institutions were set up. And that 276 judges were appointed, as well as 80 public prosecutors. Do you remember that this information is approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, as for the number of courts and public prosecutors' office, I think that this is correct. And as for the number of officials, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see the last sentence, which says -- and we are referring to mid-November 1992. It says: "The Supreme Court and the Republican public prosecutor's office have not yet started working." And then it goes on to say that there isn't yet enough staff or premises for the work of these institutions. Does the information you have correspond to what is stated here, that the public prosecutor's office, in November 1992, hadn't yet started working?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Because in 1993 I was still -- or, rather, the higher public prosecutor's office was still at the Panorama Hotel, where also a court and a basic prosecutor's office had their premises. They had come there earlier because the higher prosecutor's office was not yet in existence. That's why I think that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that structure that in 1992 and for a while even after that existed in the SFRY, apart from the judiciary as a governmental body, in all republics and autonomous provinces as well as the federal level there was also a military judiciary and there were Military Prosecutor's Offices; correct?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes. And the military ombudsman also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military judiciary and the Military Prosecutor's Offices in 1992 in the territory of the RS weren't functioning until probably autumn or even the end of the year? And when I say "functioning," I mean functioning normally.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of Justice of the RS repeatedly, due to the fact that these military bodies - that is, courts and prosecutor's offices weren't functioning - repeatedly requested that civilian courts and civilian prosecutor's offices be allowed to deal with matters and criminal offences which, under the law, were within the exclusive purview of the military judiciary and Military Prosecutor's Offices?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could the witness please be shown page 4 of this document, which is a report of the Ministry of Justice. I need paragraph 1. The sentence starts: "With regard to that" -- it's on the previous page actually, "... has accepted the duty to have regular courts deal with such crimes as would have to be dealt with by the military judiciary as the military judiciary was not functional yet."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that regular courts conducted investigative actions for criminal offences within the purview of the military judiciary? I mean, at least in the framework of the court where you were a judge.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I cannot tell whether any of my colleagues was involved in such activities. I only know that I, as a judge, was never requested to do anything of the kind, and I know that the case that we have mentioned, namely, the case of Vladimir Srebrov, was within the jurisdiction of the military court, because the Criminal Code of the SFRY stipulated that such offences are -- follow in the jurisdiction of the military court. However, I didn't know about military courts because their organisation and structure differed from those of regular courts. When I received such a request, I could not terminate the procedure. I could only state that I -- this was not in -- in my jurisdiction. And as this was a case of placing somebody in remand, into custody, I only filed a request for an investigation to be conducted. So I have no such experience, but whether anybody of my colleagues had, I cannot really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This report says that the untimely organisation of the military judiciary organs makes it more difficult for the Rule of Law to be established; and current conditions, military courts, and prosecutor's offices are mainly responsible for criminal activity since the announcement of the general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please repeat his last sentence, and let's continue from there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was too fast and have to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the question was: After I had read out this part that for acting upon criminal offences, military courts and prosecutor's offices had jurisdiction because the -- a general mobilisation had been declared, and I asked you whether or not this confirms what you told us concerning this case, the case of Mr. Srebrov. So could you now please repeat slowly the answer that you've already given me.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, because military courts had jurisdiction over criminal offences committed by military personnel as perpetrators, irrespective of the nature of the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm now going to show you document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1328.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Dated 5 August 1992. It's a letter from the Ministry of Justice to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BiH about this very problem with the military judiciary. You see that the then-minister of justice addresses the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and says that he repeats the proposal that he made in July 1992. Namely, that regular courts and public prosecutor's offices temporarily take over the jurisdiction of military courts and prosecutor's offices until the establishment of the latter. If I understood you correctly, then you're unfamiliar with this initiative of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, unfamiliar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you document -- a document that will probably also serve to illustrate this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D189.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see, this is a criminal report filed by the SJB of Vogosca on 12 December 1992. And it was submitted to the Military Prosecutor's Office of Sarajevo against one Stanko Knezevic. And he is charged with a criminal offence against prisoners of war. This person allegedly took 12 prisoners from the prison of the Vogosca Brigade and killed them. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This criminal report was sent to the Military Prosecutor's Office because it is obvious that the alleged perpetrator is a soldier, this Stanko Knezevic; correct? It says in the statement of reasons that as a member of the Semizovac Battalion, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, I was just reading the personal information. And it isn't mentioned there. But in the statement of reasons, we see that he was a member of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I think there's no contention about this involving prisoners of war, who are not members of the Serbian ethnic group; am I right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to briefly comment for us ... some documents that you've already commented when questioned by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2968, 65 ter document, shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are the log-books that you reviewed or had reviewed and then drafted a short document stating certain data from the document in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need page 3, please. 0665-0214; that's the ERN number. I don't know whether it would be possible to turn it for 90 degrees and thereby make it more easy to read. When I say "rotate," to put it upwards. Yes, thank you. Can we please zoom in on the central portion of the document, entries 26 to 30. Rather, lower part of the document is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the fifth column is the column where one enters the names of the damaged party. You told us that in many of the documents you reviewed one cannot find entries concerning the damaged party and that, therefore, you could not say whether these were persons of Serb ethnicity or non-Serb ethnicity or something different.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, it is a fact, isn't it, that all the log-books that you reviewed, KT, KTN, and the others, the log-books you reviewed in the last few days, probably over 90 per cent of perpetrators of crimes or offences logged and against whom criminal reports were brought out are people of Serb ethnicity; am I right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact percentage, but these were mostly criminal reports against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A small digression: Since you used to work also as a prosecutor, I assume you will agree with me that in order to prepare a criminal report, it is of the essence to have the damaged party, the victim, or any witness, be interviewed by the law-and-order institutions or take a -- at least a statement by such a person?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was also very common in the times of war that -- gathering of such essential information to draft a criminal report and that, at that time, it was very difficult to -- to do so, to gather this information?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: At the time, it was very difficult to conduct even the most simple of activities, let alone the more complex ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As can you see here, entry number 26, we have a legal entity. It's Han Pijesak Agricultural Society, or something like that. It is impossible to determine the ethnicity of a commercial company, and such companies can very often be found in these log-books as the damaged party. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Well, it is impossible to determine ethnic affiliation of a legal entity such as an enterprise or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at number 30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As we can see here, the damaged party is an elementary school.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 1550.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering, since questions have been asked about this particular log-book and particular entries, would this be a good time to at least mark it for identification, maybe even admit it? And the Prosecution will endeavour to get an English translation, in the near future, of it. It's not a huge log-book. But since it's obviously in the record and it's referring to particular entries, it seems appropriate to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- first of all, I -- I can't -- I thought that it was -- that it wasn't permitted to offer the document for admittance or to exhibit before we have the -- the translation. That is why I -- I was reluctant to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have admitted documents, MFI, pending translation, in earlier cases so if -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but it was my understanding, at the end of Mr. Olmsted's direct, that he will provide the list -- the Registry with the list of all these -- these documents to be MFI'd. Maybe I'm -- maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, that is -- that is a misunderstanding. I think Judge Hall and I went back and forth on that and the decision was at this time we won't even mark them for identification because the witness simply provided her results upon reviewing them. But now that we've actually brought a log-book and she's talked about that particular log-book, we could mark this one for identification, pending translation, and then that should take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D327, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While we're on this issue - and if I sound tentative, it's because I really can't remember whether this would have arisen in a private discussion that the Judges would have had among themselves or whether it arose in the colloquy between the Chamber and counsel - but did we explore the question of dealing with these log-books by - as we have done with certain other documents in the past - by eventually, for instance, in respect of this one, after it's translated, marking -- only seeking to admit one as a specimen of what all the others in the class would be? Can counsel -- do counsel remember whether we -- we did that in open court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Okay. My colleagues remind me that it wasn't -- it didn't come in open court. But this is a opportune time for counsel to consider that, because that is one of the things that we certainly consider as a means of dealing with this large volume of -- of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And you will notice, I think, we're on the same wavelength because the way we've approached these log-books so far is to only translate the headings, which tend to be the same, universally, throughout the charged municipalities, and then the particular entries that we want to ask questions about to the witness or we want those be considered by the Trial Chamber and not do the whole book. Because obviously that would overwhelm our translation resources. So I think we're basically doing exactly that. Having one that is -- more or less indicates what these log-books are all about, and then focussing on the particular log-books, the entries that are relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, when I asked you about the ethnicity of some legal entities, I believe I didn't put my question in the proper way. What I'm primarily interested in is the fact that amongst some of the entries here we have, as the damaged party, legal entities, elements of the economy. But in these KT log-books, if the damaged party is an institution or a company, an enterprise, one will -- would not see the name of the owner of, for instance, a privately-owned enterprise or a shop?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of this, even -- even if the damaged party is specified, when the party in question is a legal entity, one cannot tell whether the owner may have been a Serb or a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: For most parts, such legal entities were socially owned. They were, with the -- with the exception of shops, not owned by individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it's stated "PP" and then a name, that means a privately-owned enterprise?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When reviewing these documents, in places where you -- you saw who the damaged party was, you made your conclusions as to whether these were Serbs or non-Serbs on the basis of their name and surname, the name and surname of the person in question, which, of course, in cases you've mentioned a moment ago, need not be a correct indicator showing what ethnicity of the damaged party is.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: That is correct. But that is the only possible criterion that one can use in a log-book such as this to make an assessment. There are no other ways to determine that because there is no column defining ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecutor to assist me with something. I can see that our witness reviewed Vlasenica Prosecutor's Office KT log-book, but I'm not sure what 65 ter number that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, the Vlasenica KT is 65 ter exhibit 1552.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I have no further questions for you, madam. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Judge Gojkovic, do you recall, while you were a basic court judge in Sarajevo or a higher prosecutor, did the police ever come to you and ask for your cooperation in investigating war crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: While I was a judge at a basic court in Sarajevo, I don't remember having any official contacts with the police in relation to this topic. And while I was a senior or higher public prosecutor, I had contacts with assistant minister whose name, I think, is Goran Macar but in relation to issues relating to general crime. These were mainly offences related to general crime. Because he needed to consult us in relation to several cases, and since the seat of my office was at Pale, so the closest prosecutor -- although normally they should be consulting with basic-level prosecutors, I still think that, on several occasions, I did have contacts with Mr. Macar. But not in relation to war crimes. I don't think that was part of his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These conversations you had with Mr. Macar, could you tell us, were they in 1993 or 1994; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: I think - I assume - it was in 1994. 1994 most probably, but I cannot recollect this with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we quickly look at 65 ter 1552. It was just up on the screen a moment ago. And to save time, I want to hand the witness this log-book, which is the Vlasenica KT log-book from 1992, just so she can quickly flip through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how this came out of the cross-examination. I didn't -- I didn't pose a single question on this particular log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You -- it's not so much the log-book but the question that came up. And you'll see in a moment. But, essentially, it's your question with regard to, Were most of these crimes in these log-books against Serb perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you expect to finish today, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. After this, I'm done. And then if we can change -- turn to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Judge Gojkovic, if you could just flip through the first few pages. And can you tell me, are -- the perpetrators listed in these entries, are they Serb or are they non-Serb? And you can just flip ahead. I know you reviewed it yesterday, but just to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment. In this log-book, the first -- well, I don't how many, but certain number of persons listed are people against whom criminal reports were submitted and who are of other nationality. And, therefore, in my response when I was asked against which persons criminal reports were issued, I responded by saying that I cannot give you exact percentage but that majority of them were members of other nationalities. In this case, I think it was -- it involved illegal possession of weapons, and the reports were against members of other [as interpreted] nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm really sorry. At 73, 19, the witness says: The majority of them were member of "Serb" nationality. Not -- and it was recorded "other nationalities."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Judge, did you say the majority were of Serb nationality or majority were of non-Serb nationality? Just to clarify your answer.

utterances.speaker: Staka Gojkovic
utterances.text: The majority of people against whom, during 1992, criminal reports were submitted were of Serb ethnicity. But in this log-book for Vlasenica, there is a number of people of other nationalities against whom criminal reports were submitted. But I haven't counted them, and I don't know how many of them are mentioned in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since we've talked about this log-book as well and there is an English -- partial English translation, may this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Wasn't this the one that was marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, that was the KTN, the unknown perpetrator log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But you said partial English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Because this is quite a large log-book, and so we only translated part of it. And in this case I think it's the first entry from 19 -- from after April 1992 and the last entry from 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's mark it for identification and think it through.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1446, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Judge Gojkovic, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. And we take the adjournment to this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We take the adjournment to reconvene in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
